editorial.question: What preparation dependencies remain when LTM combines special-cell switching with secondary-cell activation?
editorial.answer: The faster command depends on prior configurations, usable pre-activation measurements and capabilities covering both cell roles; the October requests expose their alignment.
editorial.mechanism: Candidate coordination and RRC provisioning establish alternatives; MAC CE selection and activation can act on them later.
editorial.tradeoff: Preconfiguration shortens switch-time control but introduces coordination and update work; dynamic selection remains bounded by prior configurations.
editorial.consequence: Implementers need to check prepared alternatives, report availability and capability scope before treating a combined switch as an interruption reduction.
editorial.novelty: Explains the architectural reason for the October requests using the March work-item justification instead of restating the liaison.
editorial.uncertainty: Detailed capability agreements, reporting timing and RAN4 responses are unavailable; no measured latency gain is established.
editorial.analysis_excerpt: The dependency runs in both directions. A switch command that can activate secondary cells is useful only if the network has enough information to choose them. Measurements of candidate cells are useful only if the configuration and device capabilities let the network act on them. Reading the work-item description alongside the October liaisons, the open problem is whether Release 20 can connect those steps without adding a separate configuration exchange to each switch.

claims.claim: Release 20 mobility work is trying to remove a limitation of earlier fast cell switching: the network can prepare a device to change its main serving cell, but the earlier framework cannot use that same switch command to control activation of the target's secondary cells. Apple's revised work-item description identifies that limitation and proposes dynamic activation as part of the switch. The October requests from Radio Access Network Working Group 2 (RAN2) concern the measurements and device capabilities needed to make it work.
claims.passage: In addition, in Rel-18/Rel-19 the beam configuration for the UE measurement and reporting for the candidate cells in LTM is primarily with the intention of viewing that candidate cell for the role of SpCell.  While the framework does not prevent the network to use the measurements reported by the UE for SCell related evaluations, it does not provide the means for the network to control the SCell activation of the candidate target LTM cell as part of the LTM cell switch command.  If the candidate cell intends to configure Carrier Aggregation (CA) to the UE as part of it’s candidate configuration, the current framework only allows the UE to apply the CA configuration as provided in the pre-configured prior RRC configuration.

claims.claim: The work item connects this limitation to carrier aggregation: the target cell may already have supplied a configuration for additional carriers, but the switch command cannot dynamically choose their activation. Preparing the special-cell switch and preparing the secondary cells are related tasks, but they do not automatically complete together. The proposed improvement gives the network a way to select secondary-cell activation at the time of the switch, rather than simply accepting the carrier-aggregation configuration supplied earlier.

claims.claim: Layer 1/Layer 2 Triggered Mobility (LTM) was introduced in Release 18 to reduce handover interruption and latency. The revised work-item description says Release 19 extended it across central units and added event-triggered Layer 2 reporting and channel-state information reference signals. These changes expanded the framework, but retained an important dependency: candidate cells provide configurations, and the serving cell assembles the configuration delivered to the device through radio resource control (RRC) signaling.
claims.passage: As part of Rel-18, enhanced mobility feature: Layer1/Layer2 Triggered Mobility (LTM) was introduced with the aim of reducing interruption time and latency from handovers due to mobility. While Rel-18 LTM addressed the latency issues, it has limitation (for e.g., LTM was confined to intra-CU alone, mobility was based on SSB reference signals alone etc.), which were addressed in Rel-19 with further mobility enhancements with NR mobility Enhancements Phase 4 WI. Rel-19 LTM feature introduced inter-CU LTM, event triggered L2 reporting for LTM and also the ability to use CSI-RS reference signals for LTM based mobility.

claims.claim: Layer 1/Layer 2 Triggered Mobility (LTM) was introduced in Release 18 to reduce handover interruption and latency. The revised work-item description says Release 19 extended it across central units and added event-triggered Layer 2 reporting and channel-state information reference signals. These changes expanded the framework, but retained an important dependency: candidate cells provide configurations, and the serving cell assembles the configuration delivered to the device through radio resource control (RRC) signaling.
claims.passage: However, Rel-19 LTM has some shortcoming as well. The LTM framework from both Rel-18 and Rel-19 is built on the principle of network co-ordinating with potential candidate cells (from the same and inter-CU gNBs) for their configurations intended for the UE, and having the serving cell compose the net configuration and provide it to the UE to enable RRC message-less LTM switches among these candidate LTM cells. This requires extensive network node signalling to formulate the resultant RRC configuration to the UE, and if there is any change in the configuration from any of the candidate LTM cells, the co-ordination between all participating network nodes and composition by the serving cell based on the result of that co-ordination would be needed in most cases. This can be a drawback in LTM as the mobility here involves operation with beam configuration and measurement on beams from multiple candidate cells, and due to the nature of beam based mobility, there can be frequent changes on such configuration, and might require the inter-node signalling overhead and the resulting serving cell actions (on providing the updated RRC configuration), making LTM less efficient.

claims.claim: That arrangement moves preparation ahead of the switch. The device already holds candidate configurations when it receives the lower-layer instruction to change cells. However, a change in a candidate's configuration can require renewed coordination between network nodes and another composition of the device's RRC configuration. The work-item justification singles out beam configuration and measurement across candidate cells as a source of frequent changes.

claims.claim: The resulting tradeoff is between a fast switch and the work required to keep its prepared configurations usable. A short switch command does not eliminate coordination; it relies on that coordination having happened earlier. If configurations change often, the preparation process can itself become expensive. This is the architectural problem behind the Release 20 proposal to select among previously supplied measurement configurations using a control element at the medium access control layer (MAC CE).

claims.claim: For example, suppose the network has already supplied two measurement configurations for candidate cells. Selecting the second configuration through a MAC CE would avoid sending that configuration again through RRC at the point of selection. This is an illustration of the work item's proposed mechanism, not a measured latency result. The initial provisioning remains necessary, and an alternative outside the prepared set would still be outside that selection mechanism.

claims.claim: Secondary-cell activation is a separate objective in the same work item. It calls for the network to trigger activation as part of the special-cell LTM switch and to reuse candidate-cell measurement and reporting procedures where possible. It explicitly excludes early channel-state information acquisition for the secondary cell. The scope therefore supports coordinated switching and activation, without promising that every step needed to use an additional carrier has been eliminated.

claims.claim: If measurements can be obtained while a candidate is deactivated, the network can use those reports in deciding which prepared secondary cells to activate during a switch. Requiring activation before obtaining the relevant report would introduce an ordering dependency that the proposed combined operation would have to accommodate. This is a consequence of reading the measurement request against the work item's activation objective, rather than a new procedure specified in the liaison.
